Linux eBPF: The Ultimate Tracing Tool

At Devoxx France 2019, Jérémie Lagarde, a production engineer at Shopify, introduced eBPF, Linux’s powerful kernel tracing tool, in a 30-minute talk. From its origins in 1993 to its modern capabilities, eBPF enables developers to inject safe, efficient code into the kernel for performance analysis and scalability. Through live demos using the BCC toolkit and BPFtrace, Lagarde showcased eBPF’s “superpowers” for cloud, containers, and bare metal. This post explores his practical insights for developers tackling performance bottlenecks.

Understanding eBPF’s Foundations

Lagarde began by tracing eBPF’s evolution from Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF), introduced in 1993 for tools like tcpdump. BPF allowed injecting filter rules into the Linux kernel via a virtual machine with minimal registers. By 2013, eBPF extended this concept, becoming a robust kernel module with a verifier and memory controls for safe code injection. Unlike static tracepoints (available since 2004), eBPF supports dynamic probes (kprobes, uprobes) and tracepoints across kernel and user space. At Shopify, where Lagarde addressed scalability for online and physical stores, eBPF proved invaluable for tracing performance in cloud and bare-metal environments. He highlighted eBPF’s JIT compiler, optimizing injected code for efficiency, and its ability to extend kernel functionality without recompilation, a key theme at Devoxx 2019.

Harnessing the BCC Toolkit

Lagarde demonstrated eBPF’s accessibility via the BCC (BPF Compiler Collection) toolkit, which simplifies programming with Python, C, and Go bindings. He ran scripts to monitor disk latency and count kernel function calls (e.g., vfs_* functions). For instance, a Python script injected a kprobe to track vfs calls, storing counts in a kernel hash map for user-space retrieval, revealing 53 dynamic probe points. Another script analyzed CPU usage for the top command, exposing process-specific bottlenecks. These demos, executed on a Linux VM, showcased BCC’s prebuilt tools for rapid diagnostics. Lagarde emphasized their modularity, encouraging attendees to adapt scripts for specific needs, such as detecting I/O contention. The toolkit’s documentation, including a diagram of probe types, was recommended for deeper exploration, aligning with Devoxx’s hands-on focus.

Advancing with BPFtrace

For streamlined tracing, Lagarde introduced BPFtrace, a high-level language for eBPF. A single command (bpftrace -e 'kprobe:vfs_* /comm=="ls"/ { @[probe] = count(); }') replicated BCC’s VFS function counting, attaching to 53 kernel probes and filtering for the ls command. BPFtrace’s concise syntax, supporting maps and wildcards, enabled quick investigations. Lagarde also demonstrated user-space tracing, attaching a uprobe to a Java application’s JVM tracepoint (method__entry) to log method arguments, revealing runtime behavior. In a Kubernetes demo, he used a plugin to trace container functions (e.g., dc6_parent), counting 37,000 executions. Addressing an audience question, he clarified that eBPF is native to the kernel since 1993, but BCC and BPFtrace require installation (e.g., via Docker). These tools, though lightweight, demand careful production use to avoid memory overhead, reinforcing eBPF’s role in scalable systems.

To Infinity and Beyond with Angular

At Devoxx France 2019, William Marques, a full-stack consultant, delivered a 31-minute talk on scaling Angular applications while maintaining performance and clean architecture. Through live coding, he demonstrated techniques like lazy loading, AOT compilation, and feature modules, addressing common pain points in growing projects. This post recaps his strategies, offering developers practical tools to build efficient Angular applications, a key focus at Devoxx.

Structuring with Feature Modules

Marques began by addressing architectural challenges in Angular projects, where sprawling components and services degrade maintainability. Drawing from Angular’s Style Guide, he advocated for a “folder-by-feature” approach over technical layering (e.g., separate services or components folders). In a demo inspired by Angular’s “Tour of Heroes” tutorial, he organized a hero-listing feature into a heroes module, containing components (hero-list, hero-detail), services, and routes. Shared logic, like a hero model, resided in a shared module, imported across features. This structure, implemented in Angular 7, kept code modular and navigable. Responding to an audience question, Marques suggested splitting admin and user features into separate modules (admin, user), with shared services in a global shared module to optimize bundling and reuse, ensuring scalability for complex applications.

Optimizing with Lazy Loading

Performance was a central theme, as Marques cited a 2016 Google study showing 53% of users abandon sites taking over three seconds to load. He introduced lazy loading to split large JavaScript bundles into smaller, on-demand chunks. In his live-coded app, a dashboard module (975KB, including a charting library) was lazy-loaded for admin users, reducing initial load time for 90% of non-admin users. He modified the app-routing.module to use loadChildren: () => import('./admin/admin.module').then(m => m.AdminModule), creating a separate bundle. Marques also discussed preloading strategies (e.g., PreloadAllModules) to fetch modules in the background, improving navigation speed. This technique, costing minimal effort, significantly enhanced user experience, aligning with Devoxx’s focus on client-side performance.

Boosting Runtime with AOT and Tools

To address runtime sluggishness, Marques demonstrated Angular’s OnPush change detection strategy, applied to a show-user component. By setting changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush, updates occurred only when input references changed, requiring immutable objects (achieved via the spread operator). This halved refresh cycles, boosting performance for complex components. Ahead-of-Time (AOT) compilation further optimized startup by pre-compiling templates into JavaScript, reducing browser work and catching errors early (e.g., mismatched HTML bindings). AOT, enabled via ng build --aot, shaved 400ms off load time in his demo. Marques also showcased Webpack Bundle Analyzer to identify bulky dependencies (e.g., Moment.js at 500KB) and suggested Bundle Phobia for lighter alternatives. These tools, paired with his Lipitor project (integrating best practices), empowered developers to maintain lean, performant applications.

Agile is a Dirty Word: Reclaiming the Mindset

At Devoxx France 2019, James Birnie, a consultant at Thoughtworks, delivered a provocative 45-minute talk titled “Agile is a Dirty Word.” Drawing on his experience helping organizations transform, Birnie argued that agile is not a process to “do” but a mindset to embody. Misapplied frameworks, cargo cult rituals, and blame cultures have tarnished agile’s reputation, yet practical techniques can restore its value. Through analogies, real-world examples, and audience engagement, he shared strategies to foster true agility, resonating with Devoxx’s focus on cultural change.

Why Agile Feels Toxic

Birnie opened with a striking analogy, comparing organizations claiming “we’re doing agile” to countries like the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, which boast “democratic” in their names despite ranking low on the Democracy Index (e.g., 167th for North Korea). Similarly, proclaiming “agile” often masks dysfunctional practices. He recounted clients asserting, “We’ve been agile for two years,” only to reveal rigid processes far from the Agile Manifesto’s values. Agile, Birnie stressed, is a culture, not a checklist. Misconceptions equating agile with Scrum or frameworks like SAFe exacerbate the problem. SAFe’s complex diagram, with layers of architects and backlogs, exemplifies “command and control” masquerading as agility, bloating release cycles and undermining autonomy. This toxification, Birnie argued, stems from organizations adopting agile’s rituals without grasping their purpose, a theme echoed in Thoughtworks’ critiques of “fake agile.”

Cargo Cult Pitfalls

Birnie introduced the concept of cargo cults, drawing from Pacific Island communities post-World War II, who built runways mimicking American airbases to summon planes, not understanding the underlying logistics. Similarly, teams follow Scrum rituals—stand-ups, sprints—without questioning their intent, leading to cargo cult agile. He cited clients stuck in two-week release cycles, piling on testing after failed releases, drifting toward big-bang deployments despite “playing stories.” This ritualistic adherence, Birnie noted, ignores agile’s principle of simplicity. He shared a client’s excuse: “Kanban doesn’t work; we’re a special case.” Yet, no organization is unique enough to defy agile’s core values, like delivering working software frequently. By focusing on rituals over outcomes, teams miss opportunities to decouple dependencies or streamline workflows, a common frustration Birnie addressed at Devoxx.

Risk Management Theater

Birnie coined “risk management theater” to describe processes that persist without adding value, burdening agility. He shared a vivid example: a tiny piece of broken glass in a UK parking lot, cordoned off with heavy fencing for three weeks, when a dustpan could have sufficed. In software, this manifests as bloated risk management or SAFe’s PI planning, costing more than decoupling teams would. He critiqued SAFe’s “synchronization” obsession, advocating for decoupled, autonomous teams instead. Another example was a client’s dysfunctional code review process, where pull requests lingered for days, yielding stylistic nitpicks rather than quality improvements. Responding to an audience question, Birnie argued pairing delivers better outcomes than code reviews, which often become waste in distributed teams. These theatrical processes, he warned, foster blame cultures, where accountability becomes a euphemism for punishment, stifling experimentation.

Fostering a Learning Culture

To clean agile’s “dirty” reputation, Birnie proposed focusing on outcomes, not processes. He advised avoiding toxic terms like “agile” or “Scrum” in skeptical organizations, instead emphasizing Agile Manifesto principles—individuals and interactions, working software—without naming them. For example, he used value stream mapping to highlight waste (e.g., code review delays) versus value (e.g., releases), sparking discussions without mentioning agile. A low-tech MVP example—a hacker photo created with a phone torch and fizzy water—illustrated delivering value with minimal effort. Birnie also shared a success: asking a client to explain Scrum rituals’ purposes to team members, linking outcomes to personal motivations (e.g., avoiding stakeholder criticism). This small nudge improved workflows within weeks. He advocated for autonomous, cross-functional teams with clear goals and values, laminated on walls to guide decisions. A learning culture, reinforced by blame-free retros and the “retro prime directive,” replaces blame with experimentation, ensuring agile thrives. An audience question on budgeting highlighted tensions between short-termism (4.8-year UK CEO tenure) and ongoing product funding, underscoring the need for flexible budgets aligned with frequent releases.

Continuous Integration: A Partner for Test Improvement Suggestions

At Devoxx France 2019, Caroline Landry, a researcher at Inria, presented a 38-minute talk on leveraging continuous integration (CI) to enhance test quality within the STAMP project. While CI excels at running unit and integration tests to assess code quality, it often overlooks test suite weaknesses. Landry introduced two open-source Java tools—Descartes and DSpot—that automate test analysis and amplification in CI pipelines, identifying pseudo-tested methods and suggesting improvements. This post recaps her insights for developers seeking robust testing practices.

CI’s Role in Testing

Landry began by framing CI’s evolution within the STAMP project, a European initiative with academic and industrial partners focused on software testing amplification. CI automates test execution across development phases—code, build, deployment—providing rapid feedback to developers. However, while tools like linters and static analyzers catch code errors early, test quality remains underexplored. Landry noted that test suites now often surpass application code in size, yet are manually written and rarely validated. This gap prompted STAMP’s goal: amplify existing tests rather than generate them from scratch, preserving human-crafted semantics. CI pipelines, integrated with tools like Maven and Travis, are ideal for this, running tests across configurations (e.g., databases, Java versions) and supporting techniques like mutation testing. Landry emphasized that testing is omnipresent in modern DevOps, from unit tests to alpha/beta campaigns, making CI a critical partner for quality assurance, a key theme at Devoxx.

Mutation Testing with Descartes

Landry introduced mutation testing as a technique to evaluate test suite robustness, using Descartes, an extension of the PIT tool. Mutation testing injects faults (mutants) into code—e.g., changing == to !=—and reruns tests to see if they detect the changes. A surviving mutant indicates a test weakness. For a factorial function, Landry showed how a 100% code coverage suite achieved only a 60% mutation score, missing two mutants due to an absent test case. Descartes employs “extreme mutation,” proposed by Niedermayer in 2016, replacing method bodies with constants (e.g., return 1) to reduce mutant count and eliminate equivalent mutants. This revealed pseudo-tested methods—covered by tests but removable without test failures. In a singleton class example, a test verified an exception but missed behavior checks, exposing a bug. Descartes, integrated into Maven and Gradle, generates reports highlighting pseudo-tested methods and mutation scores, guiding code reviews. Landry noted its adoption in projects like XWiki, where even well-tested code harbored such methods, underscoring mutation testing’s value in CI.

Test Amplification with DSpot

To address test weaknesses, Landry presented DSpot, a tool that amplifies test suites by mutating tests themselves. Starting with a test suite and Descartes’ mutation score, DSpot applies operators like removing assertions or altering parameters (e.g., incrementing integers) to generate new tests or assertions. For instance, removing an assertion and instrumenting code to capture object states enabled DSpot to propose new assertions, improving mutant detection. In the factorial example, DSpot added a test that raised the mutation score by catching previously undetected mutants. Landry highlighted DSpot’s exploratory approach, retaining amplified tests that improve scores while discarding equivalents. Applied to open-source projects, DSpot generated tests submitted as pull requests, with 19 accepted, one rejected, and five under review, demonstrating developer trust. Integrated into CI pipelines (e.g., XWiki’s build cycle for 10 months), DSpot targets pseudo-tested methods to optimize execution time, addressing an audience concern about test readability. Landry emphasized that amplified tests are suggestions for developer review, preserving business semantics, particularly in behavior-driven development (BDD).

Industrial Integration and Feedback

Landry concluded by detailing STAMP’s CI integration, with Descartes and DSpot available as Maven plugins, Eclipse plugins, and command-line tools. A GitHub app prototype provides feedback on untested lines, though security concerns limit its public release. Partners like XWiki adopted Descartes to maintain mutation scores alongside code coverage, treating declines as CI failures. An audience question on marking classes to avoid redundant analysis prompted Landry to explain impact analysis, re-running tools only on modified code via pull requests. Another question on using mutation data to improve developer skills was acknowledged as a research avenue, though STAMP focuses on software-wide patterns. Landry invited industrial feedback to refine heuristics, like mutation operators tailored to coding practices, reinforcing STAMP’s open-source ethos. The project’s site and OW2’s documentation offer resources, aligning with Devoxx’s emphasis on practical tools.

The Genesis of Graal at Twitter

Autotune: A Machine Learning Approach to Graal Optimization

Realizing Performance Gains

Understanding Hypermedia APIs Simply Explained

In an insightful session at DevoxxFR2019, the intricacies of Hypermedia APIs were demystified, providing attendees with a clear understanding of these essential components in modern web architecture. The presentation aimed to explore the core concepts that define Hypermedia APIs, emphasizing their role in building robust and evolvable distributed systems.

The Foundation of Hypermedia APIs

Hypermedia APIs represent a fundamental shift in how web services are designed and consumed, moving beyond simple data exchange to a model where the client is guided through the application's state transitions via links embedded within the API responses. This approach, often associated with the HATEOAS (Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State) constraint of REST, ensures that APIs are self-discoverable and less brittle to changes over time. By providing actionable links, the API itself becomes the primary source of information on how to interact with it, fostering a more resilient and flexible client-server interaction.

Key Principles and Benefits

The presentation underscored several key principles of Hypermedia APIs, including the importance of explicit link relations, standardized media types for representing hypermedia, and the use of URIs to identify resources. The benefits are manifold: enhanced discoverability, reduced coupling between client and server, and improved evolvability of the API. These characteristics are particularly valuable in complex, large-scale systems where changes are frequent and maintaining compatibility is paramount. By enabling clients to dynamically discover available actions and relationships, Hypermedia APIs simplify client development and maintenance.

Practical Applications and Future Outlook

Discussing practical applications, the session would have explored how Hypermedia APIs are implemented in real-world scenarios, from enterprise applications to public-facing web services. Examples might have showcased how different hypermedia formats, such as HAL (Hypertext Application Language) or Siren, are used to structure responses and embed navigation links. The future outlook for Hypermedia APIs remains promising, as they continue to be a cornerstone for building truly RESTful and resilient distributed systems. Their emphasis on self-documentation and adaptability ensures their continued relevance in the ever-evolving landscape of web development.

Demystifying ICOs and Smart Contracts: A Practical Guide

Fabrice Plisson, a blockchain developer at Palau and a researcher at the Laboratoire d'informatique de Paris 6 (Sorbonne Université), presented an enlightening session at DevoxxFR2019, unraveling the complexities of Initial Crypto-asset Offerings (ICOs) and the foundational role of smart contracts. His presentation, aptly titled "Your ICO (shitcoin) in 15 minutes," provided a concise yet comprehensive overview of these disruptive technologies, highlighting both their potential and pitfalls.

The Core Concepts: Blockchain, Wallets, and Smart Contracts

Fabrice began by laying the groundwork with a succinct definition of blockchain: a distributed ledger, duplicated across a peer-to-peer network, governed by a consensus mechanism. He illustrated this concept as an "Excel spreadsheet" where every node holds an identical copy, ensuring transparency and immutability. The propagation of transactions, from Bob sending Bitcoin to Alice, was explained as a process of verification and ledger updates across the network until a consensus is reached among all nodes.

Accessing this distributed ledger is facilitated by "wallets," which Fabrice described as blockchain clients that store ledgers, send transactions, and continuously listen for incoming transactions to maintain an updated record. He demonstrated a practical example using MetaMask, illustrating how a transaction to transfer Ether immediately updates the balance visible on a blockchain explorer, a public interface for real-time network activity.

The discussion then transitioned to smart contracts, which Fabrice defined as programs published on the blockchain and executed on a virtual machine, akin to "stored procedures" for those familiar with traditional databases. Using Solidity, a programming language for Ethereum, he showcased a simple mathematical smart contract. These contracts, once compiled and published as assembly code onto the blockchain, are duplicated across all network nodes, allowing anyone with the contract's address to call its functions. A key distinction highlighted was the ability of smart contracts to interact with the transactional unit of the blockchain, enabling them to store, receive, and send cryptocurrency. Fabrice provided an example of a "splitter" contract designed to distribute funds to a list of recipients based on a single transaction, showcasing the automation possibilities.

Understanding ICOs and Navigating the Landscape of Crypto Investments

Building on the foundation of smart contracts, Fabrice delved into Initial Crypto-asset Offerings (ICOs), drawing an analogy to Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) but in the context of cryptocurrency. An ICO, he explained, is a fundraising mechanism where a startup creates a smart contract on the blockchain, allowing individuals to purchase "shares" or "tokens" of the company using cryptocurrency. These tokens, adhering to standards like ERC-20, define ownership (e.g., a balance table) and enable transferability, much like shares in a traditional stock market.

A crucial distinction was made between "coins" (native currency of a blockchain, like Bitcoin or Ethereum) and "tokens" (units of value issued by a smart contract and hosted on a blockchain, representing an enterprise's activity or a share). Fabrice used the analogy of cash (coins) versus shares or gift cards (tokens) to clarify this difference.

While highlighting successful ICOs like Tron, which raised significant capital and saw substantial token value appreciation, Fabrice candidly addressed the dark side: "shitcoins" and scams. He noted that the ease of launching an ICO, enabled by smart contracts, has unfortunately attracted fraudsters who exploit the credulity of investors. The workshop's provocative title, "Ton ICO (shitcoin) en 15 minutes," served as a cautionary tale, demonstrating how to create a deceptive ICO to better understand how to avoid falling victim to such schemes.

The session concluded with a Q\&A segment, where Fabrice addressed questions about the practical aspects of tokens and blockchain limitations, such as the "gas limit" for transaction sizes, and the arbitrary nature of token pricing. He emphasized that all blockchain activity is public and verifiable, allowing individuals to check transaction details and assess legitimacy.

Celebrating a Decade of "Les Cast Codeurs"

"Les Cast Codeurs," a renowned French tech podcast, celebrated its tenth anniversary at Devoxx France 2019 with a special session featuring several of its esteemed hosts. This milestone marks a decade of dedicated commitment to exploring the dynamic landscape of the Java industry and broader technology trends. The podcast, initiated by Emmanuel Bernard with the vision of sharing technological insights, has grown into a collaborative effort involving a panel of experts: Emmanuel Bernard, Guillaume Laforge, Arnaud Héritier, Antonio Goncalves, Vincent Massol, and Audrey Neveu. Their collective expertise and engaging discussions have cemented "Les Cast Codeurs" as a pivotal resource for developers and tech enthusiasts in the French-speaking community.

Streaming Apps Poison Pill: Handling the Unexpected with Kafka-Streams (Loïc DIVAD) - English Post

Navigating Data Streams: The Challenge of Poison Pills

Loïc DIVAD, a software engineer and consultant, addressed a critical challenge in real-time data processing at Devoxx France 2019: how streaming applications, particularly those built with Kafka-Streams, handle "poison pills"—undesirable or malformed messages that can disrupt an entire data flow. Apache Kafka's Streams API is a powerful library for processing large volumes of data with minimal latency, accommodating various data formats, schemas, and serialization methods. However, the presence of erroneous messages in such a high-throughput environment can lead to significant operational issues, as real-time applications cannot afford manual intervention for recovery. Loïc's presentation explored how this library is designed to manage these unforeseen events, ensuring robust and resilient stream processing.

The concept of a "poison pill" is particularly insidious in streaming architectures because a single unprocessable message can halt an entire consumer or even an entire application, leading to backlogs and data loss. Unlike batch processing, where errors can be isolated and reprocessed, real-time streams demand immediate and automated error handling. Loïc elucidated the mechanisms within Kafka-Streams that allow applications to gracefully recover from such anomalies without compromising overall performance or data integrity. His discussion was grounded in practical applications, demonstrating how various features within the StreamDSL API can be leveraged to build fault-tolerant streaming pipelines.

Robust Error Handling: Sentinel Values and Dead Letter Queues

The core of Loïc DIVAD's solution lies in advanced error management techniques, notably the use of sentinel values and dead letter queues (DLQs). Sentinel values act as specific markers within a data stream, signaling that a message, while potentially malformed, has been processed and handled in a predefined manner, preventing it from blocking the entire flow. This approach allows the stream to continue processing valid messages, while the problematic ones are flagged for further investigation or isolated handling. Loïc provided concrete examples of how to implement these values within Kafka-Streams, illustrating their effectiveness in maintaining stream continuity.

Another crucial technique discussed was the implementation of dead letter queues. DLQs are specialized topics where messages that fail processing (e.g., due to deserialization errors, validation failures, or application logic exceptions) are rerouted. Instead of crashing the application or endlessly retrying the problematic message, the poison pill is moved to a DLQ, allowing the main processing stream to proceed unhindered. This not only ensures the resilience of the streaming application but also provides a centralized location for operators to inspect, debug, and potentially reprocess erroneous messages. Loïc emphasized that while DLQs are an effective solution, their proper implementation requires careful consideration of topic configurations, consumer group management, and monitoring strategies to ensure that no critical data is inadvertently lost or ignored. He delved into the practical aspects of setting up and managing these queues, demonstrating how they integrate seamlessly with Kafka's distributed logging capabilities.

Practical Implementation with StreamDSL API

Loïc delved deep into the practical application of the Kafka-Streams StreamDSL API, showcasing how developers can programmatically implement these error handling strategies. He explained that the API provides a rich set of operators and functionalities that enable developers to build sophisticated stream processing topologies. For instance, the branch operator can be used to divert messages based on certain conditions, allowing for the isolation of malformed data. Similarly, custom deserializers and error handlers can be integrated into the stream processing pipeline to catch and manage exceptions at the earliest possible stage.

The presentation included live coding examples and architectural diagrams that clarified the flow of data through a resilient Kafka-Streams application. Loïc highlighted the importance of defensive programming within streaming applications, advocating for robust validation and type checking to minimize the occurrence of poison pills. He also touched upon the trade-offs involved in different error handling approaches, discussing how the choice between, for example, logging and skipping a message versus routing it to a DLQ depends on the criticality of the data and the business requirements. His insights provided a comprehensive guide for developers looking to build highly available and fault-tolerant streaming applications using Apache Kafka and Kafka-Streams.

MockK: The Idiomatic Mocking Framework for Kotlin (Yannick De Turck) - English Post

Rethinking Mocking in Kotlin with MockK

Yannick De Turck presented MockK at Devoxx France 2019, introducing it as an idiomatic mocking framework specifically designed for Kotlin, aiming to address the limitations often encountered when using Java-centric tools like Mockito in Kotlin projects. While Mockito is a highly effective mocking framework for Java, its approach can lead to certain inconveniences and workarounds, particularly concerning Kotlin's language features such as final classes. MockK, developed by Oleksiy Pylypenko, was created with the philosophy of providing first-class support for Kotlin features, enabling developers to write more idiomatic and cleaner Kotlin code for their unit tests.

The session served as a comprehensive introduction to MockK, highlighting its capabilities and demonstrating how to integrate it seamlessly into unit testing practices. Mocking is a crucial aspect of unit testing, allowing developers to isolate the code under test by replacing its dependencies with controlled, simulated objects. For Kotlin developers, having a framework that naturally aligns with the language's conventions and syntax is invaluable. De Turck emphasized that MockK's design simplifies the mocking process, reducing boilerplate code and making tests more readable and maintainable. This native compatibility helps in avoiding the common pitfalls of cross-language framework usage, providing a more fluid and efficient testing experience.

Features and Advantages of MockK for Unit Testing

MockK distinguishes itself by offering robust support for Kotlin-specific constructs, which include:

  • Mocking Final Classes: One of the significant pain points with Mockito in Kotlin is its inability to mock final classes by default, requiring workarounds like all-open plugins. MockK handles this natively, allowing for straightforward mocking of any class or method without additional configurations.
  • Idiomatic Kotlin Syntax: MockK's API is designed to feel natural to Kotlin developers, utilizing features like extension functions, lambdas, and named arguments, leading to more concise and expressive test code.
  • Co-routines Support: With the increasing adoption of Kotlin co-routines for asynchronous programming, MockK provides built-in support for mocking co-routine functions, a critical feature for modern Kotlin applications.
  • Verification and Argument Capturing: MockK offers flexible and powerful ways to verify interactions and capture arguments passed to mocked methods, ensuring that tests accurately reflect the expected behavior of the system.

Yannick De Turck demonstrated how these features translate into practical benefits for unit testing. By providing an idiomatic framework, MockK reduces the cognitive load on developers, allowing them to focus more on the logic of their tests rather than wrestling with framework-specific limitations. This leads to higher quality test suites, improved developer productivity, and ultimately, more reliable software. The session covered various scenarios, from basic mocking to more advanced use cases, illustrating MockK's versatility and its potential to become the go-to mocking solution for Kotlin projects.

JDK From 9 to 12: How Java is Evolving (Simon Ritter) - English Post

The Rapid Evolution of Java: JDK 9 to 12

Simon Ritter's presentation at Devoxx France 2019, "JDK From 9 to 12: How Java is Evolving," shed light on the significant transformations Java underwent due to its new six-month release cadence. This accelerated schedule has led to more major releases of Java in the preceding eighteen months than in the entire previous decade, marking a profound shift in the platform's development and delivery model. Ritter, a renowned expert in the Java ecosystem, explored these changes from both a technical perspective and in terms of their impact on the release schedule, binary distributions, and the availability of updates.

The presentation delved into the key features introduced across JDK 9, 10, 11, and 12, providing an essential overview for developers grappling with the rapid pace of change. JDK 9, in particular, was highlighted as a very significant release. While Ritter acknowledged that many in the audience were still on JDK 8, he emphasized the importance of understanding the module system introduced in JDK 9, as it is a critical aspect for migration to later releases like JDK 11, which many organizations were considering or adopting. The modularity of the JDK, essentially dividing the monolithic rt.jar file into a logical set of modules, was described as a long-overdue and necessary evolution, extending the concept of packages to a higher level of logical grouping.

Beyond the Modules: Key Features and Future Projects

Beyond the foundational changes introduced by modularity in JDK 9, Ritter also discussed other significant features across the subsequent JDK releases. While the modular system aimed to improve application structuring, reduce footprint, and enhance security, later JDK versions introduced more granular improvements and new functionalities. He touched upon features that empower developers to write more concise and expressive code, improve performance, and address modern development challenges.

The talk also looked at larger, longer-term projects designed to further enhance Java's capabilities:

  • Project Amber: Focused on language improvements, including features like var for local-variable type inference and enhanced switch expressions, aimed at making Java more readable and less verbose.
  • Project Valhalla: Concentrating on performance improvements through value types (e.g., primitives in generic types) and specialized generics, aiming to bring C++-like performance to certain Java operations by allowing objects to be stored directly in arrays, reducing memory overhead.
  • Project Loom: Explores the introduction of "fibers" (lightweight threads) to the JVM, enabling a massive increase in the number of concurrent operations without relying on operating system threads, thereby significantly improving the scalability of concurrent applications.

These projects underscore Java's ongoing commitment to innovation, addressing historical limitations, and adapting to modern software development paradigms, from cloud-native architectures to microservices. Ritter's session provided a valuable roadmap for understanding not just the current state of Java but also its trajectory towards a more efficient, scalable, and developer-friendly future.

Kotlin Under the Covers: Unveiling Hidden Mechanics (Chet Haase, Romain Guy) - English Post

Diving Deep into Kotlin's Core

At Devoxx France 2019, Chet Haase and Romain Guy, both from Google's Android team, presented "Kotlin Under the Covers," a session designed to demystify some of Kotlin's powerful language features. While Kotlin is celebrated for its conciseness and developer-friendliness, many of its conveniences can obscure the significant work happening behind the scenes, including object allocations and reflections. This dynamic isn't always obvious from the Kotlin code itself, prompting the presenters to explore how developers can uncover these hidden mechanics and understand their implications for code performance and efficiency.

Haase and Guy aimed to achieve two primary goals with their talk: first, to explain how these Kotlin features work at a lower level, providing insights into their compilation and runtime behavior; and second, to equip developers with tools and techniques to discover this information about their own code. They emphasized that understanding what happens "under the covers" is crucial, especially in performance-critical sections of an application. The session, though presented by Android developers and often using Android-specific tools for examples, highlighted that the concepts and debugging techniques discussed are broadly applicable to any Kotlin project.

Unveiling Bytecode and Optimization Strategies

The core of Haase and Guy's exploration involved delving into the bytecode generated by the Kotlin compiler. By examining the intermediate bytecode, developers can gain a precise understanding of how Kotlin code is translated into instructions executable by the JVM, revealing potential performance bottlenecks or unexpected behaviors. This technique allows for a deeper analysis beyond the high-level Kotlin syntax, exposing the underlying operations like object creation and method calls that might otherwise remain hidden.

The presentation also touched upon tools and strategies for optimizing Kotlin code, particularly in the context of the Android ecosystem. They mentioned that Google works closely with the Kotlin team, and there are ongoing efforts to address some of the identified "under the covers" issues. Optimizers, such as R8 (a tool similar to ProGuard for Android), play a crucial role in reducing the overhead introduced by certain Kotlin features, further enhancing the performance and efficiency of applications. Understanding these underlying mechanisms and available tools empowers developers to make informed decisions about their code, ensuring that they leverage Kotlin's power without inadvertently compromising performance. The session served as a valuable guide for developers looking to optimize their Kotlin applications by gaining a clearer understanding of how the language operates at a fundamental level.

The Rise of the Web: A Historical Perspective (Loïc Ortola) - English Post

Tracing the Web's Ascent: From Applets to JavaScript Dominance

At Devoxx France 2019, Loïc Ortola presented "The Rise of the Web," a captivating historical journey that unraveled the evolution of web technologies and explained how the web, as we know it, came to dominate the digital landscape. The talk aimed to bridge the knowledge gap for those who didn't experience the early days, delving into the foundational shifts that shaped today's internet. Ortola challenged the notion that Sun Microsystems initially believed Java Applets would replace HTML, a significant historical detail that highlights the divergent paths early web technologies almost took.

The presentation explored various pivotal moments, including the origins of "Mozilla," the fierce "browser wars" that shaped the competitive landscape of web browsers, and the emergence of the application server. It meticulously traced the beginnings of dynamic web content and the eventual ascendancy of JavaScript, a language once dismissed for anything beyond trivial web effects. Ortola underscored the ironic shift: from a time when Java application servers were preferred for serious web development, to today, where Flash and Applets have vanished, entirely superseded by modern web technologies. This historical perspective provides crucial context for understanding the current state of web development and the forces that propelled the web to its current omnipresence.

Key Milestones and Technological Shifts

Ortola's narrative meticulously chronicled the key milestones that contributed to the Web's rise. He began in 1969 with Ken Thompson's invention of Unix, noting the initial absence of networked computers and the isolated nature of early systems. The emergence of DARPA and its focus on network resilience marked a turning point, leading to the development of foundational networking concepts.

The talk then progressed through the significant events that paved the way for the modern web:

  • The birth of the World Wide Web: Tim Berners-Lee's invention of the WWW at CERN in 1990, establishing the core protocols and technologies that define the web.
  • Mosaic and Netscape: The release of the Mosaic browser in 1993, which democratized access to the web, followed by the founding of Netscape and the subsequent "browser wars" against Microsoft's Internet Explorer.
  • The rise of JavaScript: Initially created for client-side interactivity, JavaScript's utility dramatically expanded with the advent of technologies like Ajax and Node.js, solidifying its role as a full-stack language.
  • The demise of plugins: The decline of Flash and Java Applets, which were once dominant for rich internet applications, in favor of open web standards like HTML5, CSS3, and modern JavaScript APIs.

By detailing these technological shifts and the cultural impact they had, Ortola provided a comprehensive overview of how the web transformed from a niche academic tool into a global platform. His presentation served as a valuable reminder of the iterative nature of technological progress and the surprising turns that lead to today's ubiquitous digital experiences.

Designers, Developers: Creating the Difference (Florent Berthelot, Cécile Freyd-Foucault) - English Post

Bridging the Gap: Designers and Developers Collaborating for Unique Interfaces

At Devoxx France 2019, Florent Berthelot, a web developer, and Cécile Freyd-Foucault, a designer, presented a collaborative approach to creating distinctive and coherent user interfaces. Their talk, "Designers, Developers: Creating the Difference!," addressed a common challenge in the industry: the homogenization of websites due to the widespread use of ready-made component libraries like Material Design and Bootstrap. While these libraries offer practical, off-the-shelf design systems, they often result in projects lacking personality and differentiation.

Berthelot and Freyd-Foucault, both from Zenika, highlighted the problem with a vivid illustration: three different websites (news, e-commerce for sails, travel) all exhibited a striking resemblance, using similar components and design principles. This pervasive uniformity stems from the tendency to adopt existing UI toolkits at the project's outset, leading to a lack of unique identity. Their session proposed methods and techniques for design and development teams to imbue their projects with a unique identity, ensuring interfaces are not only consistent and pleasant but also distinct from the pervasive "sameness."

Crafting Identity Through Iterative Design and Atomic Design Principles

The core of their proposed solution revolved around an iterative approach to design and development, starting with establishing a project's unique identity. They emphasized that instead of simply adopting a pre-made design system, teams should actively define their brand's visual language and integrate it into their component library. The presenters introduced their custom application, "Aqua Compose," as a practical example to demonstrate how to build a unique user interface by carefully selecting and composing elements, rather than relying on generic solutions.

Their methodology aligns with the principles of Atomic Design, a methodology that advocates for building interfaces from the ground up, starting with fundamental elements (atoms) and progressively combining them into more complex structures (molecules, organisms, templates, and pages). This systematic approach allows for greater control over the design process, ensuring consistency and brand identity across all interface elements. Berthelot and Freyd-Foucault showcased how to:

  • Define Identity: Explore and establish the unique visual characteristics of a project, including colors, fonts, and iconography, which are foundational to brand identity.
  • Implement Functional Elements: Translate the defined identity into functional UI components.
  • Develop an Adapted Design System: Rapidly build a customized design system that adheres to Atomic Design principles, allowing for iterative refinement and adaptation throughout the project lifecycle.

By fostering better communication between designers and developers and embracing these iterative and component-based design methodologies, teams can overcome the challenge of generic interfaces and create truly differentiated user experiences. Their talk provided a compelling argument for investing in bespoke design systems, even incrementally, to infuse projects with distinctiveness and character.

Kata Retrospective: Exploring Java 11’s Functional Side

At Devoxx France 2019, Rémi Forax, a Java contributor and professor at Université Paris-Est Marne-la-Vallée, delivered a 47-minute interactive session titled “Kata Retrospective en Java 11.” Instead of a traditional lecture, Forax guided attendees through a coding kata to explore Java 11’s functional programming capabilities. Participants built a parser API using lambda expressions, Optional, and Java 11’s enhancements like List.copyOf. Through mob programming and a retrospective, Forax demonstrated how to design functional APIs, aligning with Devoxx’s hands-on ethos.

Kata-Driven Exploration

Forax’s session was unconventional, encouraging attendees to complete a kata beforehand on GitHub (forax/kata-retrospective-11). The kata tasked participants with building a parser API that processes strings based on regular expressions (regex), returning parsed values (e.g., integers via Integer.parseInt) or nothing if unmatched. Forax framed this as an abstraction of chained if-else statements, aiming for a functional design. He introduced the parser as a Parser<T> interface, taking a string and returning an Optional<T>. Using Eclipse, Forax live-coded solutions, engaging the audience in mob programming. He humorously noted null-handling issues, emphasizing early validation with Objects.requireNonNull. The kata’s collaborative nature, with Forax joking about test failures, fostered a dynamic learning environment, showcasing Java’s evolution toward functional paradigms.

Functional Design with Optional

The parser’s design leveraged Java 8’s Optional to handle cases where a string matches a regex or fails, embodying the railway pattern—a term coined by Scott Wlaschin for functions returning multiple states (value or absence). Forax defined Parser<T> with a single abstract method, Optional<T> parse(String text), enabling lambda implementations. For example, an empty parser returns Optional.empty() via a lambda: text -> Optional.empty(). He implemented methods like from(Pattern pattern) to match regex and extract groups, using Optional.of(matcher.group(1)).filter(Matcher::matches). The map method transformed parsed strings (e.g., to integers), requiring careful type variance with ? super T and ? extends R. Forax highlighted Optional’s monadic nature, chaining operations like filter and map to avoid explicit null checks, a functional approach that simplified error handling and resonated with Devoxx’s focus on modern Java.

Java 11 Features in Action

Forax showcased Java 11’s enhancements, emphasizing their role in cleaner, functional code. The List.copyOf method, introduced in Java 10, ensured defensive immutable copies of regex and mapper lists, preventing mutations post-construction—a bug he caught during coding. Java 9’s Optional.or method allowed chaining parsers: if one fails, another tries, via parse(text).or(() -> otherParser.parse(text)). Local variable type inference (var) streamlined declarations, though Forax quipped about his Eclipse habits revealing his “age.” He critiqued Java’s wildcard types (? extends, ? super), suggesting future compiler improvements could infer variance, a nod to Project Amber. These features, combined with Java 8’s streams and lambdas, enabled concise, expressive code, though Forax noted Java’s “fake functional” nature due to underlying object-oriented interfaces.

Optimizing with a Single Automaton

The kata’s second part addressed performance. Initially, each regex created a separate automaton, leading to inefficiencies. Forax proposed combining regexes into a single automaton using String.join("|", regexes), reducing overhead. This required storing regex and mapper lists, validated for equal sizes and non-null elements. A bug surfaced: mutable lists risked post-construction changes, necessitating List.copyOf. Forax implemented a new parser class, compiling the combined regex once and mapping matches to values via indexed mappers. This optimization, while complex, showcased Java’s balance of functional abstraction and practical performance, aligning with Devoxx’s emphasis on real-world applicability. The session ended with a lighthearted birthday nod to an attendee, reinforcing the community spirit.

First Steps in Deep Learning with Keras

In a concise 15-minute talk at Devoxx France 2019, Loïc Mathieu, a consultant at Zenika, introduced deep learning with Keras in “Mes premiers pas en deeplearning avec Keras.” Targeting beginners, Mathieu shared his three-day journey into neural networks, demonstrating image classification and similarity search for retail applications. Using Keras with Python, he showcased practical prototypes, emphasizing simplicity and real-world potential, a fitting addition to Devoxx’s accessible tech talks.

Keras for Image Classification

Mathieu’s journey began at a retail company, where he explored deep learning during innovation days. Using Keras, a high-level Python library atop TensorFlow, he built a neural network to classify clothing images (e.g., sportswear vs. evening wear). He explained neural networks as layers of nodes processing features—numerical inputs like pixel values. For images, convolution layers extract patterns (e.g., edges), followed by max-pooling to reduce data while retaining key features. Mathieu used the pre-trained VGG16 model, with 16 layers, removing its final layer to retrain on 2800 clothing images (60% training, 40% validation). With just six lines of code, he achieved 95% accuracy, leveraging Keras’ ImageDataGenerator to compute image features. This simplicity, Mathieu noted, makes Keras ideal for rapid prototyping, aligning with Devoxx’s practical focus.

Image Similarity Search

Mathieu’s second prototype enabled Google-like image similarity search for retail catalogs. Using VGG16’s feature extraction (minus its classification layer), he indexed images as numerical representations. A new image’s features were compared against the catalog using cosine similarity, retrieving the ten closest matches. For example, a plaid shirt image returned similar shirts, though results varied with external images, prioritizing pose or color over clothing type. Mathieu highlighted limitations: inconsistent image formats (e.g., flat vs. worn) confused the model, requiring preprocessing. The prototype, built for a hackathon, became a mobile app API, though Mathieu left the company before its completion. This use case underscored Keras’ versatility for retail innovation, engaging Devoxx attendees with tangible applications.

Consul@Criteo: From Machines to Service Mesh (Pierre Souchay) - English Post

Managing a Vast Infrastructure with HashiCorp Consul

Pierre Souchay's presentation at DevoxxFR2019, "Consul@Criteo: Des services un peu, des machines beaucoup, du ServiceMesh bientôt," offered a deep dive into how Criteo leverages HashiCorp Consul for service discovery within its extensive infrastructure. Criteo operates a massive environment with over 15,000 distinct service types running on more than 30,000 nodes, distributed across 8 data centers. This scale presents significant challenges in terms of managing service communication, load balancing, and overall system resilience.

The talk highlighted Consul's pivotal role in enabling a hybrid architecture at Criteo, where containers and physical machines coexist and interoperate seamlessly. Souchay detailed the evolution from a system reliant on dedicated physical machines to a more dynamic service-oriented architecture. This shift involved transforming fixed physical topologies into flexible, dynamic virtual ones, allowing for greater agility and scalability in deploying and managing applications. Consul's service discovery capabilities are fundamental to this transition, providing the necessary mechanisms for services to locate and communicate with each other efficiently, regardless of their underlying infrastructure.

Load Balancing Evolution and Open Source Contributions

Beyond service discovery, Pierre Souchay elaborated on Criteo's multifaceted approach to load balancing. The company employs a variety of mechanisms to distribute traffic across its infrastructure, including traditional hardware load balancers like F5, software-based solutions like HaProxy, and modern Client Side Load Balancing libraries. This diversified strategy underscores the complexity of managing traffic flows in a high-volume, low-latency advertising environment.

Souchay also shed light on Criteo's future direction towards adopting a Service Mesh architecture, with Consul playing a central role in this transition. Service Mesh is an increasingly popular pattern for managing inter-service communication, providing features like traffic management, policy enforcement, and observability at the infrastructure layer. A significant aspect of Criteo's work with Consul is their commitment to open source. Souchay proudly noted that Criteo has become a leading external contributor to the Consul project, with numerous optimizations and enhancements developed internally being merged back into the upstream open-source version. This collaboration benefits the wider community, improving Consul's performance and robustness for other large-scale deployments. The presentation offered valuable insights for both developers and operations professionals looking to understand real-world architectural visions beyond basic product overviews.

Natural Language Processing on Text in 2019 (Alexis Agahi) - English Post

The State of the Art in NLP: From Basics to Deep Learning

Alexis Agahi's presentation at DevoxxFR2019, "Traitement Automatique du Langage sur du texte en 2019," offered a comprehensive overview of Natural Language Processing (NLP) mechanisms applied to text, reflecting the state of the art in 2019. The talk was structured to guide the audience through the evolution of information comprehension and extraction from text, starting with fundamental concepts that lay the groundwork for understanding NLP. Agahi then progressed to explain the major advancements brought about by the advent of Deep Learning, which significantly transformed the field.

Deep Learning models, particularly neural networks, have enabled NLP to achieve remarkable feats in tasks such as sentiment analysis, machine translation, text summarization, and question answering. Agahi's session provided insights into how these advanced techniques, moving beyond traditional rule-based or statistical methods, empower systems to better understand and process human language. The discussion covered various architectural innovations and algorithms that contribute to the enhanced capabilities of modern NLP systems, making complex language tasks more approachable and accurate.

The Revolution of Unsupervised Language Models

A particularly intriguing segment of Agahi's presentation focused on recent publications from late 2018 concerning unsupervised learning for the production of language models. These developments, which some experts consider a revolution in the NLP field, mark a significant shift towards training models on vast amounts of unlabeled text data. Traditional supervised learning approaches require large, meticulously labeled datasets, which are often expensive and time-consuming to create. Unsupervised methods, by contrast, can learn representations of language patterns from raw text without explicit labels, opening up new possibilities for scaling NLP capabilities.

Agahi highlighted the impact of these unsupervised models, such as BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers), which have demonstrated unprecedented performance across a wide range of NLP tasks. These models learn context and meaning by predicting masked words or understanding sentence relationships within large corpora. The ability to pre-train powerful language models on generic text and then fine-tune them for specific tasks with much smaller labeled datasets has democratized access to high-performance NLP, making it more accessible to a broader range of applications and developers. Agahi's talk effectively conveyed the excitement and potential surrounding these advancements, emphasizing their transformative impact on the landscape of natural language processing.

Discovering Bazel: Google's Build Tool (Paul Boutes) - English Post

Demystifying Bazel: Philosophy and Positioning

Paul Boutes's session at DevoxxFR2019, "À la découverte de Bazel," aimed to demystify Bazel, Google's internal build tool that was open-sourced in 2015. For many curious developers, Bazel's presence in the build tool ecosystem can be enigmatic, often perceived as complex or difficult to approach. Boutes tackled these perceptions head-on, exploring Bazel's core philosophy and positioning it relative to other popular build tools.

The talk highlighted Bazel's key promises: fast, reliable, and hermetic builds. A "hermetic" build ensures that the build output is identical regardless of the environment in which it's run, by isolating it from external factors like installed tools or environment variables. This characteristic is crucial for reproducibility and consistency in large-scale software development. Boutes explained that while the learning curve for Bazel can be steep, especially for those accustomed to tools like Gradle or Maven, the investment pays off in terms of build efficiency and correctness. He also acknowledged that Bazel's tooling was still evolving in 2019, but emphasized the strong backing from major players like Google, Databricks, and Stripe, indicating a promising future for the tool.

Practical Concepts and Multi-Language Capabilities

The presentation delved into the practical aspects of working with Bazel, making its foundational concepts more accessible. Boutes covered essential elements such as BUILD files, which define build targets and dependencies, and the creation of comprehensive dependency graphs that ensure all necessary inputs are available. He also introduced the concepts of rules (which define how specific types of artifacts are built), workspaces (the root directory for a Bazel project), and the Bazel query language for inspecting the dependency graph.

One of Bazel's most powerful features highlighted in the session is its ability to handle multi-language compilation. This makes it ideal for polyglot repositories where projects might involve Java, Python, C++, or JavaScript within the same codebase. Boutes also demonstrated how Bazel can be used for testing across these diverse languages and even for advanced tasks like creating Docker images without relying on Docker itself, showcasing Bazel's versatility in managing complex build processes. The session provided a valuable roadmap for developers to begin exploring Bazel and understand its potential to streamline and optimize their build pipelines for large-scale, multi-language projects.

jq: Mastering JSON Like a Pro

At Devoxx France 2019, Sébastien Lecacheur, an architect at a contact center software provider, delivered a 30-minute talk titled “jq, JSON comme un pro.” Lecacheur introduced jq, a powerful command-line tool for manipulating JSON, demonstrating its ability to simplify tasks like data extraction and transformation. Using Star Wars-themed JSON datasets, he showcased jq’s Unix-inspired design and functional programming approach, making it a must-know tool for developers navigating JSON-heavy environments.

JSON Challenges in Modern Development

JSON’s ubiquity in APIs, configurations, and databases has made it a cornerstone of development, yet its raw form—often a dense, unformatted stream—poses challenges. Lecacheur highlighted how developers traditionally resorted to tools like sed or grep to parse JSON, yielding clunky results. Unlike XML’s xmlstarlet or HTML’s CSS selectors, JSON lacked a dedicated tool until jq emerged. Released in 2015 with version 1.6 by 2018, jq offers a lightweight, open-source solution for Linux, macOS, and Windows. Its online playground (jqplay.org) lets users test expressions interactively, reinforcing its accessibility for tasks like API data extraction or web scraping.

jq Essentials: Filters, Operators, and Constructors

Lecacheur introduced jq’s core concepts: filters, operators, and constructors. Filters extract data, like the identity filter (.) to return the input JSON or .name to fetch a field’s value. Nested projections (e.g., .results[0].name) access deeper structures, while [] iterates arrays. Operators like the pipe (|) chain filters (e.g., .results | .[0]), mimicking Unix pipelines, and the comma (,) combines outputs. Constructors build new JSON, such as {name: .name} for objects or [.name] for arrays. Using a Star Wars API dataset with 87 characters, Lecacheur demonstrated extracting Luke Skywalker’s attributes, showcasing jq’s concise, expressive syntax for real-world API workflows.

Advanced JSON Manipulations

Beyond basics, Lecacheur explored advanced jq features. The select function filters data based on conditions (e.g., .results | select(.gender == "male")), while group_by aggregates by fields, like counting characters by gender (19 females, one hermaphrodite). He showed how to diff JSON exports by sorting attributes (--sort-keys) and arrays (sort_by(.title)), reducing a 4285-line diff to two meaningful changes. Splitting JSON into files by gender or merging multiple files into one highlighted jq’s ETL-like capabilities. Custom functions, stored in .jq files, further streamline repetitive tasks. Lecacheur’s demos underscored jq’s role in simplifying complex JSON operations, earning praise from attendees for its Unix philosophy.

IoT Security: Moving Beyond Fear to Practical Solutions

In a 15-minute quickie at Devoxx France 2019, Paul, an IoT evangelist, tackled IoT security myths in “Sécurité IoT et si on arrêtait de se faire peur pour passer au concret ?” Drawing parallels to early internet hysteria, he urged developers to adopt an engineering mindset, focusing on actionable security measures rather than sensationalized threats. By categorizing attack types and proposing simple solutions, Paul offered a grounded perspective for building secure IoT devices.

Debunking IoT Security Fear

Paul likened 2019’s IoT security discourse to 1990s internet fears, where exaggerated stories—like hacked bank accounts—stifled progress. He clarified that many IoT devices, like security cameras, are just internet-connected PCs with outdated systems, not true IoT. Real IoT devices, like autonomous sensors with 10-year lifespans, face unique challenges, such as limited bandwidth for updates. Paul debunked high-profile attacks, like the Jeep hack requiring physical access or thermostat ransomware needing an SD card insertion, emphasizing that exploitability matters more than vulnerability. His humorous analogy—using a baseball bat for car theft—highlighted the need to contextualize risks.

Practical Security Tips for IoT

Paul advocated for service-based business models to fund ongoing updates, warning developers against working for companies relying on one-off sales, which often lead to unmaintained devices. He recommended specifying security requirements in design contracts, as embedded systems lack standardized frameworks. Encryption is non-negotiable, with all modern IoT protocols supporting it natively; Paul advised adding custom security layers, like HTTPS over WEP, for longevity. For physical attacks, low-cost solutions like resin encasing or binary-stored keys deter casual hackers. He stressed slowing attackers rather than aiming for impregnability, likening it to an alarm system that diverts thieves elsewhere, a pragmatic approach resonating with Devoxx’s engineering focus.

Cloud-Native CI/CD with Knative and Tekton Pipelines

Andrea Frittoli, an open-source advocate at IBM, delivered a 46-minute talk at Devoxx France 2019 titled “Cloud Native CI/CD with Knative and Tekton Pipelines.” Frittoli explored how Knative and Tekton simplify cloud-native CI/CD, addressing the complexity of microservices and service meshes. Through demos and insights, he showcased automated workflows, from scaling serverless services to triggering pipelines via GitHub events, highlighting reproducibility and community-driven innovation.

Challenges of Cloud-Native Development

Cloud-native applications, with their microservices and service meshes, offer flexibility but complicate development workflows. Frittoli noted that verifying small changes across numerous components is daunting without automation. Knative, launched in 2018, provides a serverless platform with serving, eventing, and build components, while Tekton, spun off from Knative in March 2019, focuses on CI/CD pipelines. Hosted by the Continuous Delivery Foundation, Tekton integrates with tools like Jenkins X, enabling developers to streamline testing, deployment, and scaling across Kubernetes clusters, a key concern for Devoxx attendees.

Knative: Serverless Abstractions

Knative’s serving component enables services to scale to zero, conserving resources when idle, and auto-scale based on request metrics. Its abstractions—service, configuration, revision, and route—support multiple code versions, allowing traffic splits (e.g., 50% to revision A). Eventing defines sources (e.g., GitHub webhooks) and channels (e.g., Kafka-backed) to trigger services. Frittoli demonstrated a dashboard app with JavaScript and Python layers, scaling from zero pods to active services on demand. Despite a network hiccup, the demo illustrated Knative’s ability to manage dynamic workloads, aligning with cloud-native principles.

Tekton: Flexible CI/CD Pipelines

Tekton introduces pipeline abstractions: tasks (with sequential steps as containers), pipelines (task combinations), and pipeline runs (runtime executions). Resources, like Git repositories or cluster credentials, bind inputs and outputs. Frittoli showcased a pipeline building a Docker image via Kaniko, a tool for reproducible builds without privileged containers. Tasks run in parallel across nodes, sharing data via persistent volume claims. A demo triggered a pipeline run from a Knative service definition, executing linters and tests before deploying a new revision, demonstrating Tekton’s role in automating complex CI/CD workflows.

Integrating Knative and Tekton

Frittoli highlighted Knative-Tekton synergy, where Knative’s serving triggers Tekton pipelines for new revisions, and eventing decouples pipeline stages (e.g., test results processing). A custom Go “glue” application processed GitHub events, creating pipeline runs dynamically. This reproducibility—using identical tasks locally and in CI/CD—reduces surprises, though pipeline execution can be slower than instant-feedback tools. Attendees asked about Tekton’s web UI (in development) and cluster separation (recommended for CD). Frittoli emphasized community-driven task libraries as key to Tekton’s future, reinforcing open-source collaboration at Devoxx.

10 Things I Wish I Knew Before Using Spark in Production

At DevoxxFR2019, Hien Arora and N. N. Yadav delivered a highly practical and insightful presentation titled "10 Things I Wish I Knew Before Using Spark in Production." This session was specifically tailored for developers struggling with prolonged Spark job execution times, offering a treasure trove of best practices, optimizations, and fine-tuning techniques refined over years of production experience. Hien and N. N. shared invaluable strategies to accelerate Spark jobs and minimize resource consumption. Their discourse encompassed advanced Spark tuning, data serialization formats, storage formats, hardware optimizations, parallelism control, resource manager configurations, improved data locality, and Garbage Collection (GC) optimization. They also guided the audience on the appropriate use of RDD, DataFrame, and Dataset to fully leverage Spark's internal optimizations.

Optimizing Spark Performance

Hien and N. N. commenced by addressing common pitfalls that lead to sluggish Spark job completion. A significant portion of their talk was dedicated to sophisticated Spark tuning techniques. They emphasized the critical importance of caching data when it is accessed multiple times to avoid redundant computations, suggesting that storing frequently used data in memory is always beneficial. They also presented the option of using off-heap memory as an alternative, acknowledging that while it might introduce a slight performance overhead due to increased latency, it effectively mitigates out-of-memory issues for executors. This practical advice directly impacts job efficiency and stability in production environments. Furthermore, they underscored the necessity of selecting appropriate data serialization formats to optimize data transfer and storage, which significantly impacts overall performance.

Resource Management and Data Locality

The discussion then shifted to effective resource management and ensuring optimal data locality. The speakers highlighted how careful configuration of resource managers can dramatically influence Spark's efficiency. They cautioned against over-allocating resources for streaming applications, pointing out that providing excessive resources might be counterproductive if the event inflow isn't consistently high. This is crucial for avoiding wasteful resource utilization and ensuring that resources are scaled appropriately to the actual workload. They reiterated the importance of data locality, explaining how keeping computation close to the data minimizes network traffic and improves processing speed. While they acknowledged that certain hardware configurations might depend on the specific event throughput, their general recommendations on resource allocation and data placement are universally applicable for enhancing Spark job performance and ensuring stable operations in a production setting.

Micronaut: Dragon-Slayer (Spring/boot) or Just Another Framework?

At DevoxxFR2019, V. Dejanovic explored the landscape of modern Java frameworks with a deep dive into Micronaut, posing the provocative question: is it a "Dragon-Slayer" to Spring/Spring Boot, or merely another contender in the crowded field? Spring has long dominated the Java world, celebrated for its power and versatility, but this strength often comes with a performance cost. Vladimir's presentation meticulously examined Micronaut, a framework that promises comparable power to Spring but without the associated overhead. The session aimed to provide a comprehensive comparison, highlighting how Micronaut stacks up against Spring and whether it truly lives up to its bold claims.

Understanding the Core Differences: Micronaut vs. Spring

V. Dejanovic initiated the discussion by dissecting the fundamental architectural divergences between Micronaut and Spring. He emphasized that the core distinction lies in their approach to dependency injection and aspect-oriented programming. Spring typically performs much of its heavy lifting at runtime through reflection, leading to larger memory footprints and slower startup times. In contrast, Micronaut leverages compile-time annotation processing to generate the necessary code, resulting in significantly faster startup times, lower memory consumption, and smaller application sizes. Vladimir detailed how this compile-time optimization is a game-changer for cloud-native applications, serverless functions, and microservices, where rapid startup and minimal resource usage are paramount. This shift in paradigm, Vladimir argued, allows Micronaut to deliver comparable feature sets to Spring while offering superior performance characteristics, particularly crucial in a world moving towards highly distributed and elastic architectures.

Performance Benchmarks and Real-World Implications

Beyond the theoretical underpinnings, Vladimir presented compelling performance benchmarks that showcased Micronaut's advantages in real-world scenarios. He provided concrete examples demonstrating Micronaut's superior startup times and reduced memory usage compared to Spring Boot applications. These metrics are not just academic; they translate directly into tangible benefits for production deployments, such as faster deployments, reduced cloud infrastructure costs, and improved responsiveness for demanding applications. Vladimir highlighted that while Spring remains a powerful and mature framework, Micronaut offers a compelling alternative for projects where resource efficiency and rapid iteration are critical. The discussion underscored that the choice between the two frameworks often comes down to specific project requirements, with Micronaut emerging as a strong contender for high-performance, cloud-native solutions.

The Ecosystem and Future Outlook of Micronaut

V. Dejanovic also addressed the breadth of Micronaut's ecosystem and its future trajectory. He showcased Micronaut's comprehensive support for various technologies, including reactive programming, message queues, and database integrations, demonstrating its capability to build full-fledged enterprise applications. Vladimir noted that despite being a newer framework, Micronaut has rapidly built a robust community and a rich set of integrations. He concluded by discussing the potential for Micronaut to continue gaining traction, particularly as organizations increasingly prioritize efficiency and scalability in their microservices architectures. Vladimir’s insights suggested that while Micronaut might not completely "slay" the Spring "dragon," it certainly offers a powerful and efficient alternative that is well-suited for the evolving demands of modern software development, presenting a compelling case for its adoption in new projects.

Coroutines and Reactive Programming: Friends or Foes?

At DevoxxFR2019, K. Kamiński delivered an insightful presentation titled "Coroutines and Reactive Programming - friends or foes?" This session delved into a crucial debate in asynchronous application development, examining whether coroutines can entirely replace reactive programming, if developers should exclusively use coroutines, or if a synergistic approach combining the best of both worlds offers a superior solution. Konrad's talk meticulously explored the fundamental differences between coroutines and reactive programming, identifying scenarios where each excels and delving into the underlying design decisions that influence their performance and interoperability. The goal was to provide clarity on when to leverage each paradigm for optimal results.

Fundamental Differences and Use Cases

Konrad began by dissecting the core distinctions between coroutines and reactive programming. He explained that while both paradigms facilitate asynchronous operations, they do so with fundamentally different approaches. Coroutines, particularly in Kotlin, offer a more sequential and imperative style of writing asynchronous code, making it often appear as straightforward as synchronous code while still allowing for non-blocking execution. Reactive programming, on the other hand, embraces a data-stream-oriented model, focusing on the propagation of data changes and the composition of asynchronous operations through operators. Konrad elaborated on specific use cases where one might shine over the other; for sequential asynchronous tasks, coroutines often lead to cleaner, more readable code, whereas reactive programming excels in scenarios involving complex event streams and data flows, allowing for powerful transformations and compositions.

Performance, Interoperability, and Design Decisions

A significant portion of Konrad's presentation focused on the performance implications and interoperability between coroutines and reactive programming. He explored how the underlying design decisions of each paradigm affect their efficiency and how well they can coexist within a single application. Konrad highlighted that coroutines generally exhibit lower overhead for simple asynchronous operations due to their lightweight nature, while reactive streams might introduce more overhead in certain contexts due to their broader event-driven model. He also delved into the mechanisms for bridging the two, demonstrating how developers can convert between coroutine-based flows and reactive streams, enabling a hybrid approach that leverages the strengths of both. This discussion provided valuable insights into how developers can make informed decisions about which paradigm to choose based on performance requirements and existing architectural patterns, ensuring optimal resource utilization and responsiveness.

Synergistic Approaches and Future Trends

Konrad concluded by advocating for a synergistic approach, suggesting that rather than viewing coroutines and reactive programming as mutually exclusive, developers should consider how they can complement each other. He proposed that by understanding the strengths and weaknesses of each, one could select the most appropriate tool for a given task or even combine them within a single application to achieve superior results. Konrad emphasized that the evolving landscape of asynchronous programming encourages flexibility and pragmatism. He touched upon future trends and the ongoing development in both areas, indicating that the interoperability between these paradigms is likely to improve further, offering even more powerful and expressive ways to build highly concurrent and responsive applications. This nuanced perspective provided attendees with a roadmap for navigating the complexities of modern asynchronous programming, fostering a pragmatic approach to design and implementation.
